notes.title: 1.1 Definition of Management
notes.content:
• Management is the process of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling the resources of an organisation (human, financial, physical, informational) to achieve its goals efficiently and effectively.
• Definitions:
– Mary Parker Follett: "the art of getting things done through people."
– Henri Fayol: "To manage is to forecast and plan, to organise, to command, to coordinate and to control."
– F.W. Taylor: "knowing exactly what you want men to do and then seeing that they do it in the best and cheapest way."
– Peter Drucker: "management is a multi-purpose organ that manages a business and manages managers and manages workers and work."
– Harold Koontz: "the art of getting things done through and with people in formally organised groups."
– Stoner: "the process of planning, organising, leading and controlling the efforts of organisation members and of using all other organisational resources to achieve stated organisational goals."
• Three views of management: as a process (functions), as a discipline/ field of study, as a group of people (the managers).
• Resources managed (the 5 Ms): men, money, materials, machines, methods (plus minutes/ time and markets in some lists).
• Administration vs management: Administration (determination of objectives and broad policies — top-level function, thinking) vs management (execution of policies — middle/lower level, doing). Oliver Sheldon, Theo Haimann and Peter Drucker use different views; today they are used interchangeably.

notes.title: 1.2 Nature and Characteristics of Management
notes.content:
• Goal-oriented: achieves organisational objectives.
• Universal: applies to all organisations — business, government, hospitals, schools, NGOs.
• Multi-dimensional: management of work, people and operations.
• Continuous process: an ongoing series of functions.
• Group activity: needs a team to achieve common goals.
• Dynamic: adapts to environmental changes.
• Intangible force: cannot be seen but its effect is visible in results.
• Authority–responsibility relationship; decision making; integrating human, physical and financial resources.
• Is management a science, an art or a profession?
– Science: has a systematic body of knowledge, principles based on experiments (Taylor's experiments, Hawthorne), universal validity (but principles are flexible and not as exact as in pure sciences — a "soft/inexact/behavioural science").
– Art: application of knowledge to achieve results — personal skill, creativity, practice, perfection comes with experience (manager's leadership skill is individual).
– Profession: requires specialised knowledge, formal education (MBA), a representative body (AIMA, AMA), a code of conduct, service motive — but lacks restricted entry, a legally enforced code and a monopoly; management is thus an emerging profession.
– Conclusion: management is both a science and an art, and is evolving as a profession.
• Levels of management: top, middle, lower (see 1.4).
• Importance: achieves group goals; increases efficiency; creates a dynamic organisation; helps achieve personal objectives; develops society (employment, quality products).
• Objectives: organisational (survival, profit, growth), social (benefit to society), personal (employee needs).

notes.title: 1.3 Efficiency and Effectiveness in Management
notes.content:
• Efficiency: doing the task correctly — getting the maximum output from minimum inputs ("doing things right"); concerned with means; input–output ratio.
• Effectiveness: completing the task and achieving goals ("doing the right things"); concerned with ends.
[TABLE]
Basis | Efficiency | Effectiveness
Meaning | Doing the task in the right way with minimum resources | Doing the right task and achieving objectives
Focus | Means (inputs and process) | Ends (outputs/ results)
Concerned with | Cost reduction, waste avoidance | Goal accomplishment
Measure | Output ÷ input | Actual result vs target
Example | Producing 100 units with Rs 5,000 | Producing the product that customers want
[/TABLE]
• A manager must be both efficient and effective. High efficiency without effectiveness = producing the wrong product at low cost. Effectiveness without efficiency = achieving goals at high cost.
• Productivity = output ÷ input — links both.

notes.title: 1.4 Managerial Levels and Skills
notes.content:
• Top-level management (board of directors, chairman, CEO, MD, president): determine objectives, policies and strategies; integrate organisation with its environment; responsible to shareholders; long-term planning; mainly conceptual and human skills.
• Middle-level management (departmental heads, divisional managers, plant managers): translate top-level plans into operational plans; coordinate; motivate lower level; tactical decisions; human and conceptual/technical skills.
• Lower (first-line/ supervisory/ operational) level (foremen, supervisors, section officers): directly supervise workers; day-to-day operations; ensure quality and quantity; solve workers' problems; technical and human skills.
• Skills of managers (Robert L. Katz, 1955):
– Technical skill: knowledge of and proficiency in a specific method or process — highest need at the lower level.
– Human (interpersonal) skill: ability to work with, understand and motivate people — equally needed at all levels.
– Conceptual skill: ability to see the organisation as a whole, think abstractly and plan strategically — highest at the top level.
– Later additions: diagnostic, analytical, communication, political, design skills.
• Levels vs skills: top — mostly conceptual; middle — a balance; lower — mostly technical.

notes.title: 1.5 Functions of Management
notes.content:
• Fayol's five functions: planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling. Koontz and O'Donnell: planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling. Gulick and Urwick (POSDCORB): planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting, budgeting. Stoner: planning, organising, leading, controlling.
• 1. Planning: deciding in advance what to do, how, when and who will do it; setting objectives and choosing a course of action; bridge from where we are to where we want to be.
• 2. Organising: assigning tasks, grouping activities into departments, delegating authority, establishing relationships and coordinating.
• 3. Staffing: filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure — manpower planning, recruitment, selection, training, appraisal, compensation.
• 4. Directing (leading): instructing, guiding, motivating and supervising people — includes supervision, motivation, leadership, communication.
• 5. Controlling: measuring actual performance against standards and correcting deviations.
• Coordination: the essence of management — synchronising individual efforts to achieve common objectives; not a separate function but running through all.
• Characteristics of the functions: interrelated and continuous; performed at all levels (with varying emphasis); universal. Decision making is an integral part of each.

notes.title: 1.6 Mintzberg's Ten Managerial Roles
notes.content:
• Henry Mintzberg (1973, "The Nature of Managerial Work") studied what managers actually do and identified ten roles in three categories:
[TABLE]
Category | Role | Description
Interpersonal | Figurehead | Ceremonial and symbolic duties (receiving visitors, signing documents)
Interpersonal | Leader | Hiring, training, motivating subordinates
Interpersonal | Liaison | Maintaining a network of contacts outside the unit
Informational | Monitor | Seeking and receiving information; scanning the environment
Informational | Disseminator | Passing information to subordinates
Informational | Spokesperson | Transmitting information to outsiders on behalf of the organisation
Decisional | Entrepreneur | Initiating change and improvement projects
Decisional | Disturbance handler | Dealing with unexpected crises
Decisional | Resource allocator | Allocating money, time, people
Decisional | Negotiator | Representing the organisation in negotiations
[/TABLE]
• Findings: managers work at a fast pace in fragmented bursts, prefer verbal communication, and the roles are interlinked.

notes.title: 1.7 Evolution of Management Thought: Pre-Classical Thoughts
notes.content:
• Pre-industrial/ early management: ancient practices — Egyptians (pyramids), Chinese (Sun Tzu's "Art of War"), Roman Catholic Church (hierarchy), Kautilya's Arthashastra (state administration), Venetian arsenal, Adam Smith (1776) — division of labour (pin factory example) in "Wealth of Nations".
• Industrial Revolution (18th century): factory system created need for management of large organisations — problems of labour, supervision, productivity.
• Pre-classical contributors: Robert Owen (1771–1858) — "father of modern personnel management"; improved working conditions, reduced working hours and raised the minimum working age of children at the New Lanark mills, and described workers as "vital machines" deserving as much care as physical machines. Charles Babbage (1792–1871) — "On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures" — division of mental labour, time study, profit-sharing, "Babbage principle"; Andrew Ure (education for managers); Charles Dupin; Henry Poor; Daniel McCallum (organisation charts for railways).
• Classical period: scientific management (Taylor), administrative management (Fayol), bureaucracy (Weber).

notes.title: 1.8 Classical Approach: Scientific Management (F.W. Taylor)
notes.content:
• Frederick Winslow Taylor (1856–1915) — "Father of Scientific Management"; books: "Shop Management" (1903) and "Principles of Scientific Management" (1911); worked at Midvale Steel and Bethlehem Steel (pig iron handling experiment with Schmidt; shovel experiment).
• Definition: "science of management" — the application of scientific methods to management problems for maximum efficiency and prosperity for both employers and employees.
• Four principles of scientific management:
– 1. Science, not rule of thumb: replace guesswork with scientific study of each task (one best way).
– 2. Harmony, not discord: cooperation between management and workers; a "mental revolution".
– 3. Cooperation, not individualism: workers and managers should work together.
– 4. Maximum output in place of restricted output and development of every worker to his greatest efficiency and prosperity (scientific selection and training).
• Techniques of scientific management:
– Time study: measuring the time taken to do a task with a stopwatch to set a standard.
– Motion study: analysing the motions of a job to eliminate wasteful ones (Gilbreths).
– Fatigue study: rest periods.
– Standardisation: of tools, materials, methods, conditions, products.
– Differential piece-rate system: higher rate for those who meet or exceed standard, lower rate for those who do not (e.g. 120% for ≥ standard; 80% below).
– Functional foremanship: eight specialised foremen — four in planning (route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, shop disciplinarian) and four in production (speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector).
– Scientific selection and training; separation of planning and doing; mental revolution; exception principle.
• Contributors:
– Frank and Lillian Gilbreth: motion study; "therbligs" (18 basic motions — Gilbreth spelt backwards); bricklaying (reduced motions from 18 to 5); "one best way".
– Henry L. Gantt: Gantt chart (bar chart for scheduling work against time); task and bonus wage system; humanised scientific management.
– Harrington Emerson: "12 principles of efficiency"; efficiency engineering.
– Morris Cooke, Carl Barth, Henry Ford (assembly line).
• Criticism: treated workers like machines (economic man); ignored human and social needs; led to monotony and unemployment; opposed by trade unions; weakened workers' initiative; ignored role of management beyond production; concentrated on the shop floor; supposed one best way; the Hoxie Report (1915) criticism; workers feared layoffs.
• Significance: foundation of industrial engineering, work study, productivity, wage incentives, standardisation, selection and training.

notes.title: 1.9 Administrative Management (Fayol), Bureaucracy (Weber)
notes.content:
• Henri Fayol (1841–1925): French mining engineer; "Father of Modern (Administrative) Management"; book "Administration Industrielle et Générale" (1916); focused on top-level management.
• Six activities of an industrial enterprise: technical (production), commercial (buying/ selling), financial, security (protection), accounting, managerial.
• 14 principles of management:
[TABLE]
No. | Principle | Meaning
1 | Division of work | Specialisation increases efficiency
2 | Authority and responsibility | Right to give orders and the obligation to deliver; should be equal
3 | Discipline | Obedience, respect and observing agreements
4 | Unity of command | One employee receives orders from one superior only
5 | Unity of direction | One head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
No. | Principle | Meaning
6 | Subordination of individual interest to the general interest | Organisation's interest first
7 | Remuneration | Fair and satisfactory pay for employer and employee
8 | Centralisation (and decentralisation) | Appropriate balance of decision-making authority
9 | Scalar chain | Line of authority from top to bottom; Fayol's gang plank (bridge) permits cross-communication
10 | Order | "A place for everything and everything in its place" — material order and social order
11 | Equity | Kindness and justice to employees
12 | Stability of tenure of personnel | Avoid unnecessary turnover
13 | Initiative | Freedom to think out and execute a plan
14 | Esprit de corps | "Union is strength" — team spirit and harmony
[/TABLE]
• Fayol vs Taylor: Taylor — shop floor, scientific approach, specialist; Fayol — top management, general theory, administrative; Taylor: "Father of scientific management"; Fayol: "Father of administration/ general management".
• Other contributors: Luther Gulick and Lyndall Urwick (POSDCORB), James D. Mooney (coordination, scalar principle), Chester Barnard (cooperative system; "The Functions of the Executive", 1938; acceptance theory of authority).
• Bureaucracy — Max Weber (1864–1920): German sociologist; "ideal type" of organisation based on rational-legal authority.
– Types of authority: traditional (customs, inheritance), charismatic (personal qualities of the leader), legal-rational (rules and laws — bureaucracy).
– Features (principles) of bureaucracy: division of labour; clear hierarchy of authority; formal written rules and procedures; impersonality; employment based on technical qualification (merit); career orientation; separation of ownership from management; written records.
– Merits: efficiency, predictability, fairness, rule-based, specialised. Demerits: red tape, rigidity, slowness, depersonalisation, resistance to change, "bureaucratic dysfunctions", goal displacement; unsuited to dynamic environments.

notes.title: 1.10 Human Relations Movement and Behavioural Approach
notes.content:
• Reasons for emergence: classical theories neglected the human factor; growth of trade unions; findings of the Hawthorne studies.
• Hawthorne Experiments (1924–1932), Western Electric Company, Chicago — Elton Mayo (Harvard) and Roethlisberger, Dickson:
– 1. Illumination experiments (1924–27): varying lighting showed output rose in both test and control groups — lighting was not the main factor.
– 2. Relay assembly test room (1927–29): six women assemblers; changes in rest breaks, hours, snacks; output rose regardless — due to attention, group cohesion and a sense of importance (the Hawthorne effect).
– 3. Mass interviewing programme (1928–30): 20,000 employees interviewed; showed importance of social needs and feelings; informal organisation.
– 4. Bank wiring observation room (1931–32): men's group set its own output norm; informal group norms influence output more than financial incentives.
– Conclusions: the workplace is a social system; informal groups influence behaviour; social and psychological factors (recognition, participation) motivate more than money alone; good supervision and communication matter; workers are not "economic man" but "social man".
• Contributors: Mary Parker Follett ("prophet of management" — "law of the situation", integration, power-with rather than power-over), Chester Barnard, Kurt Lewin (group dynamics, change process).
• Behavioural (Behavioural Science) Approach (1950s onwards): studies why people behave as they do using psychology, sociology and anthropology — motivation (Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor, Vroom, McClelland, Alderfer, Adams), leadership (Likert, Blake and Mouton, Fiedler), group dynamics, Chris Argyris (immaturity–maturity theory), Rensis Likert (Systems 1–4), organisational development.
• Criticism of human relations: overemphasis on informal groups and "happy worker = productive worker"; ignored the economic and structural factors; weak research.

notes.title: 1.11 Modern Approaches: Quantitative, Systems and Contingency
notes.content:
• Quantitative (management science/ operations research) approach: uses mathematical models, statistics and computer simulation for decision making — linear programming, queuing, PERT/CPM, decision trees, inventory models, game theory, MIS. Evolved during World War II (operations research). Features: decision-centred, mathematical, computer-aided. Limitations: ignores human factors; models are simplifications; costly; needs skills.
• Systems approach: an organisation is a system — a set of interrelated, interdependent parts working together to achieve goals.
– Concepts: inputs → transformation (process) → outputs with feedback; subsystems; open system (interacts with the environment) vs closed system; synergy (the whole is greater than the sum of the parts); entropy; equifinality; boundaries; holism. Contributors: Ludwig von Bertalanffy (General System Theory), Kast and Rosenzweig, Katz and Kahn.
– Benefits: integrated view of the organisation and its environment; shows interdependence of departments. Limitations: abstract; difficult to apply.
• Contingency (situational) approach: there is no "one best way"; the best management style depends on the situation ("it all depends"). Contributors: Joan Woodward (technology and structure), Tom Burns and Stalker (mechanistic vs organic organisations), Lawrence and Lorsch (differentiation and integration), Fred Fiedler (contingency model of leadership), Hersey–Blanchard. Merits: flexible, realistic, integrates earlier approaches. Demerits: lacks a unifying theory; difficult to identify all situational variables.
• Other modern approaches: Total Quality Management (Deming, Juran), McKinsey 7-S, Learning organisation (Senge), Business Process Re-engineering, Knowledge management, Management by Objectives (Drucker), Peters and Waterman's "In Search of Excellence", Theory Z (Ouchi).

notes.title: 2.1 Planning: Meaning, Definition, Nature and Significance
notes.content:
• Planning: the process of deciding in advance what to do, how to do it, when to do it and who is to do it; selecting objectives and the policies, procedures and programmes to achieve them. (Koontz: "bridging the gap from where we are to where we want to go.") Fayol: "to foresee and provide means for the future." Billy Goetz: "Planning is fundamentally choosing."
• Nature/ features:
– Goal-oriented (primary function); primary function of management (precedes other functions); pervasive (all levels, all departments); continuous (a continuous process); futuristic (looks ahead; forecasting); involves decision making (choice among alternatives); mental exercise (thinking and intelligence); flexible; integrated (plans of departments are coordinated).
• Significance (importance):
– Provides direction; reduces uncertainty; reduces overlapping and wasteful activities; promotes innovative ideas; facilitates decision making; establishes standards for controlling (planning and controlling are inseparable — "twin blades of scissors"); coordination; efficient use of resources; better preparation for contingencies; motivates employees.
• Limitations: leads to rigidity; may not work in a dynamic environment; reduces creativity; involves huge costs; time-consuming; does not guarantee success; planning premises may be wrong; resistance; lack of accurate information; psychological barriers.
• Planning vs forecasting; planning vs budgeting.

notes.title: 2.2 Types of Plans
notes.content:
• Koontz and O'Donnell's hierarchy of plans:
– Mission/ purpose: the basic reason for the existence of the enterprise.
– Objectives (goals): the end results to be achieved; SMART — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
– Strategies: a comprehensive plan to achieve organisational objectives — determine long-term direction and allocation of resources; formulated by top management in the light of the environment and competition.
– Policies: general statements/ understandings that guide thinking in decision making — broad guidelines (e.g. promotion from within; credit policy; pricing policy).
– Procedures: a chronological sequence of steps to be followed in performing a task (e.g. procedure for purchase, recruitment, handling of grievances).
– Methods: the prescribed way in which one step of a procedure is to be performed.
– Rules: specific, definite statements of what must or must not be done; no flexibility (e.g. "No smoking").
– Programmes: a comprehensive plan including goals, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources and sequence for a set course of action (e.g. a recruitment drive).
– Projects: a single-use set of activities with a definite start and end (e.g. building a plant).
– Budgets: statements of expected results expressed in numerical (financial) terms.
• Classification:
– By time: long-range (strategic), medium-range, short-range (operational).
– By level/ function: strategic plans (top management, long-term, whole organisation), tactical (administrative) plans (middle management, medium-term, departmental), operational plans (lower management, short-term, day-to-day).
– By use: single-use plans (programmes, projects, budgets — used once) and standing plans (policies, procedures, methods, rules — used repeatedly).
– By specificity: specific vs directional (flexible); contingency plans (alternate plans).
[TABLE]
Basis | Policy | Procedure | Rule
Nature | Guideline for thinking and action | Sequence of steps | Strict command
Flexibility | Some discretion allowed | Step-by-step; limited discretion | No discretion
Scope | Broad | Narrower | Narrowest
Example | Recruit from within | Steps of recruitment | No smoking
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 2.3 Planning Process and Premises
notes.content:
• Steps in the planning process:
– 1. Being aware of opportunities (environment scanning — SWOT analysis).
– 2. Setting objectives (for the whole organisation, then for each department).
– 3. Developing premises (assumptions about the future conditions).
– 4. Identifying alternatives.
– 5. Evaluating alternatives (cost–benefit, risk, resources).
– 6. Selecting an alternative (decision making).
– 7. Formulating derivative (supporting) plans (budgets, schedules, programmes).
– 8. Implementing the plan.
– 9. Follow-up and review (monitoring).
• Planning premises: the assumptions or forecasts about the future on which plans are based — the foundation of planning.
– Classification: Internal (within the organisation — policies, resources, capital investment, management ability, labour relations, organisation structure) vs External (outside — economic, political, legal, technological, social, competitors, government policy, market conditions).
– Tangible (quantifiable — sales volume, costs, capital) vs intangible (not quantifiable — employee morale, public image).
– Controllable (can be influenced — company policy), semi-controllable (market share), uncontrollable (weather, inflation, government decisions).
– Forecasting techniques: time series, regression, Delphi technique, market surveys, expert opinion, scenario analysis, trend extrapolation.
• Tools of environment analysis: SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses — internal; Opportunities, Threats — external), PESTLE (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental), BCG matrix (stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs), Porter's five forces, GE matrix, Ansoff matrix.

notes.title: 2.4 Policies and Procedures; Limitations of Planning
notes.content:
• Policies: formulated by top management; characteristics: clear, consistent, flexible, in writing, uniform, derived from objectives, widely communicated. Types: originated, appealed, imposed (by government), implied; organisational vs functional policies (production, marketing, finance, personnel).
• Procedures: details the step-by-step course of action; characteristics: chronological; routine; prevents duplication; specific to each department; example — purchase procedure: requisition → inquiry → quotations → order → receipt → inspection → payment.
• Difference between policy and strategy: policy — a guide to decision making within set limits; strategy — a comprehensive plan for long-term competitive advantage.
• Overcoming limitations of planning: involve employees, build flexibility (contingency plans), ensure accurate information, use scientific forecasting, regular review, balance between costs and benefits.

notes.title: 2.5 Decision Making: Importance and Types
notes.content:
• Decision making: the process of choosing the best alternative from the available alternatives to achieve objectives. (Peter Drucker: "Whatever a manager does he does through decision making"; Herbert Simon: "decision making is synonymous with managing".)
• Importance: the essence of managerial work; selecting objectives; basis of all functions; ensures organisational efficiency; influences the success; a guide to action; provides uniformity; accountability; motivates employees.
• Characteristics: selection of the best alternative; goal-oriented; a mental process; a continuous activity; commitment to action; involves time and risk; positive or negative (choice not to act).
• Types of decisions:
– Programmed decisions (routine, repetitive, structured; rules and procedures; low level; e.g. issue of stores, salary payment) vs Non-programmed decisions (unique, non-repetitive, unstructured; top level; judgement and creativity; e.g. new product launch, merger).
– Strategic (long-term, top level, major resources), tactical/ administrative (middle), operational (day-to-day, lower).
– Organisational vs personal; basic (fundamental) vs routine; individual vs group (committee) decisions; policy vs operating; major vs minor.
– Decision-making environment: certainty, risk, uncertainty (and ambiguity).
[TABLE]
Basis | Programmed | Non-programmed
Nature | Routine, repetitive | Unique, new
Structure | Well defined, rules | Ill-defined
Level | Lower/ middle | Top
Basis for decision | Policies/ procedures | Judgement/ creativity
Risk | Low | High
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 2.6 Decision-Making Process, Styles and Models
notes.content:
• Herbert Simon's three phases: Intelligence (identify problem), Design (develop alternatives), Choice (select the best).
• Steps of the rational decision-making process:
– 1. Identify the problem (definition and diagnosis — find real cause).
– 2. Identify decision criteria (and their weights).
– 3. Develop (generate) alternatives.
– 4. Analyse and evaluate alternatives (advantages, disadvantages, cost, risk, tools).
– 5. Select the best alternative.
– 6. Implement the decision.
– 7. Evaluate (follow up) the results (feedback).
• Models: Rational (classical) model — complete information, optimising; Bounded rationality (Simon) — limited information and cognitive capacity, so managers "satisfice" (accept a satisfactory solution); Administrative model; Intuitive/ retrospective; Garbage can model; Incremental model (Lindblom — "muddling through"); Vroom–Yetton–Jago model for group decision (autocratic, consultative, group).
• Decision-making styles:
– Rowe and Mason's four styles: Directive (low tolerance of ambiguity, rational and fast — focus on the short term), Analytical (high tolerance, rational; seeks more information), Conceptual (high tolerance, intuitive; creative, long-term), Behavioural (low tolerance, intuitive; supportive of people).
– Autocratic (manager decides), consultative, participative/ democratic, consensus; individual vs group.
• Group decision making: advantages — more information and knowledge, diversity of views, acceptance and commitment, legitimacy; disadvantages — time-consuming, conformity pressure (groupthink), dominance by one member, ambiguous responsibility. Techniques: brainstorming, nominal group technique, Delphi technique, electronic meeting, devil's advocate.
• Tools: decision tree (expected monetary value), SWOT, cost–benefit analysis, break-even analysis, linear programming, PERT/CPM, simulation, payoff matrix; decision criteria under uncertainty: maximin (Wald), maximax, minimax regret (Savage), Hurwicz, Laplace.
• Expected monetary value (EMV) = Σ (payoff × probability).

notes.title: 2.7 Decision-Making Errors and Biases
notes.content:
• Heuristics: mental shortcuts that can cause systematic biases.
• Common biases/ errors:
– Overconfidence bias: overestimating one's ability/ knowledge.
– Anchoring bias: relying too heavily on the first piece of information.
– Confirmation bias: seeking only information that supports one's view.
– Availability bias: judging by easily recalled examples.
– Representativeness bias: judging by similarity to stereotypes.
– Hindsight bias: believing after the event that it was predictable.
– Framing effect: the way information is presented affects choice.
– Sunk-cost fallacy and escalation of commitment: continuing a failing course because of past investment.
– Randomness error: seeing patterns in random events.
– Self-serving bias: attributing success to oneself and failure to external causes.
– Immediate gratification bias, groupthink, status-quo bias, loss aversion, optimism bias.
• Other errors: wrong problem definition, insufficient information, ignoring alternatives, poor implementation, ignoring risks, emotional decisions.
• Remedies: be aware of biases; seek diverse opinions; use data and structured processes (checklists, decision matrices); pre-mortem analysis; devil's advocate; decision logs; slow down; follow up and learn from feedback.

notes.title: 3.1 Nature and Purpose of Organising
notes.content:
• Organising: the process of identifying and grouping the work to be performed, defining and delegating authority and responsibility, and establishing relationships to enable people to work together effectively. (Koontz: "the establishment of an intentional structure of roles".) Organisation (as a structure) — framework of authority and relationships; organising (as a process) — creating that framework.
• Features: division of work; grouping of activities; coordination; authority–responsibility relationships; common objectives; a continuous process; a dynamic function; structure showing who reports to whom.
• Purpose/ importance: benefits of specialisation (division of labour); clarity in working relationships; optimum use of resources; coordination; adaptation to change; effective administration; development of personnel; expansion and growth; avoids duplication and confusion.
• Steps in the process of organising: (1) identification and division of work; (2) departmentalisation (grouping); (3) assignment of duties; (4) establishing reporting relationships (hierarchy); (5) delegation of authority; (6) coordination.
• Departmentalisation — bases: functional (production, marketing, finance, HR), product, territory/ geographic, customer, process/ equipment, time (shift), project/matrix, number.

notes.title: 3.2 Principles of Organising and Types of Organisational Structures
notes.content:
• Principles of organising: division of labour; unity of objective; unity of command; scalar chain; span of control; delegation; parity of authority and responsibility; balance; continuity; flexibility; efficiency; simplicity; coordination; unity of direction; exception; clarity.
• Formal organisation: deliberately created structure with defined rules, hierarchy and relationships. Informal organisation: network of social relationships among members — emerges spontaneously (friendship, groups); effects: fast communication (grapevine), satisfaction of social needs, may support or oppose management.
[TABLE]
Basis | Formal Organisation | Informal Organisation
Origin | Deliberately created | Spontaneous
Authority | From top | From group/ social acceptance
Structure | Hierarchy, rules | No fixed structure
Communication | Official channels | Grapevine
Basis of behaviour | Rules, job | Personal relations
[/TABLE]
• Types of organisational structure:
– 1. Line organisation (scalar, military type): authority flows from top to bottom in a straight line; each person reports to one superior. Merits: simple, unity of command, quick decisions, discipline, low cost. Demerits: overburdened line managers, lack of specialisation, rigidity, autocratic. Suitable for small firms/ armed forces.
– 2. Functional organisation (Taylor): functional foremen/ specialists each in a function; more than one boss. Merits: specialisation, efficiency. Demerits: violates unity of command, confusion, difficult discipline.
– 3. Line and staff organisation: line authority + staff specialists who advise (no command authority). Staff types: personal, specialised, general. Merits: expert advice, relieves line managers, balanced decisions. Demerits: friction between line and staff, cost, staff may lack accountability.
– 4. Divisional (product/ territory) structure: divisions — each division is self-contained with its own functional units; used by large diversified firms (e.g. Tata, Reliance). Merits: accountability, focus, easier expansion. Demerits: duplication of resources, inter-division rivalry, high cost.
– 5. Matrix organisation: a grid combining functional and project/ product structures — dual command (two bosses); used in aerospace, construction, consulting. Merits: flexibility, optimum use of specialists, teamwork. Demerits: dual authority conflicts, complexity, stress.
– 6. Project organisation: temporary, task-force based.
– 7. Committee organisation: a group of persons assigned to perform a task collectively. Types: line, staff, executive, standing (permanent), ad hoc (temporary), formal, informal. Merits: group decision, coordination, representation of interests. Demerits: time-consuming, costly, indecision, dominance, diffused responsibility.
– 8. Network/ virtual organisation, team-based, boundaryless, flat organisation, hourglass structure.
• Tall vs flat structure: Tall — narrow span, many levels, slower communication, more control; Flat — wide span, few levels, quicker communication, more autonomy.
• Line vs staff:
[TABLE]
Basis | Line | Staff
Authority | Command and decision | Advisory and service
Function | Direct achievement of objectives | Support
Example | Production manager | HR/ legal adviser
Relationship | Superior–subordinate | Advisor–advisee
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 3.3 Authority, Delegation, Centralisation and Decentralisation
notes.content:
• Authority: the legal or formal right to give orders, make decisions and take action; flows from top to bottom; Power: the ability to influence others (may be informal). Responsibility: the obligation to perform assigned duties; flows from bottom to top. Accountability: being answerable for results; cannot be delegated. Principle: authority must be commensurate with responsibility.
• Types of authority: line, staff, functional authority. Sources of power (French and Raven's five bases): legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent.
• Delegation: the downward transfer of authority to a subordinate to carry out a task while the manager remains accountable. Elements: assignment of duty (responsibility), granting of authority, creation of accountability.
– Process: (1) assign duties; (2) grant authority; (3) create obligation/ accountability; (4) follow-up.
– Importance: reduces manager's burden; develops subordinates; quick decisions; motivation; efficiency; basis of organisation; helps expansion.
– Principles of delegation: results expected; parity of authority and responsibility; unity of command; absoluteness of responsibility; exception principle; clarity of authority.
– Barriers: on manager's side — fear of loss of power, fear of competition, perfectionism, lack of confidence in subordinates; on subordinate's side — lack of confidence, fear of criticism, absence of incentives; on organisation's side — lack of clear structure.
– Delegation vs decentralisation: delegation is a process between a superior and subordinate; decentralisation is a policy of systematic dispersal of authority throughout the organisation.
• Centralisation: concentration of decision-making authority at the top; Decentralisation: systematic delegation of authority to lower levels.
[TABLE]
Basis | Centralisation | Decentralisation
Authority | Concentrated at the top | Dispersed to lower levels
Decision making | Slow, from top | Faster, at lower levels
Suitable for | Small organisations; crisis | Large, diversified organisations
Uniformity | High | Possible variation
Development of managers | Limited | Encouraged
Cost of control | Lower | Higher
[/TABLE]
• Factors determining the degree of decentralisation: size, history, philosophy of management, availability of managers, technology, geographical spread, diversity of products, environment, control techniques, cost and importance of decision.

notes.title: 3.4 Span of Control
notes.content:
• Span of control (span of management): the number of subordinates who can be effectively supervised by one superior.
• Narrow span — tall structure; wide span — flat structure. Optimum span is not fixed (often 4–8 at top, 8–15 at lower levels according to the school).
• Graicunas' formula (V.A. Graicunas, 1933): the number of possible relationships = n[2^(n−1) + (n − 1)], where n = the number of subordinates (the three kinds of relationship counted are direct single, direct group and cross relationships). Example: n = 3: 3[4 + 2] = 18; n = 4: 4[8 + 3] = 44; n = 5: 5[16 + 4] = 100; n = 6: 6[32 + 5] = 222. It shows relationships (direct single, cross, and group) increase geometrically.
• Factors affecting span: nature of work (routine — wider), ability of manager and subordinates, nature of the organisation, similarity of work, clarity of plans, delegation, communication systems, geographical dispersion, degree of control, availability of staff assistance, motivation, time available.
• Relationship between span of control and levels: inverse — narrower span = more levels (tall); wider span = fewer levels (flat).

notes.title: 3.5 MBO and MBE
notes.content:
• Management by Objectives (MBO): a participative process in which managers and subordinates jointly set objectives, define each person's responsibilities in terms of results and use the objectives as guides for operating and assessing performance. Popularised by Peter Drucker (1954, "The Practice of Management"); developed by George Odiorne and John Humble.
– Steps: (1) set organisational goals; (2) set departmental and individual objectives jointly; (3) action plans; (4) periodic performance review; (5) feedback; (6) appraisal and reward; (7) set new objectives.
– Features: participative goal setting; measurable results; time frame; joint review; self-control; links individual and organisational goals.
– Benefits: clarity; motivation and commitment; better planning and control; improved communication; objective appraisal; development; coordination; use of resources.
– Limitations: time-consuming and paperwork; difficulty in setting quantifiable goals; overemphasis on short-term and quantity; rigid in a changing environment; conflict between goals; lack of top-management commitment; fear of failure.
• Management by Exception (MBE): a control principle in which the manager's attention is focused only on significant deviations (exceptions) from standards; routine matters are handled by subordinates. Originally from F.W. Taylor's exception principle.
– Steps: set standards and tolerance limits; measure performance; compare; identify significant exceptions; investigate and take corrective action.
– Benefits: saves manager's time; focus on critical areas; encourages delegation; reduces information overload; improves decisions. Limitations: requires accurate standards; may miss small recurring problems; subordinates may hide issues; needs good information systems; may discourage initiative.
– MBO vs MBE: MBO — proactive, goal-based, participative; MBE — focuses on deviations, a control technique.
[TABLE]
Basis | MBO | MBE
Focus | Achievement of objectives | Deviations from standards
Nature | Participative and proactive | Control-based and reactive
Time | Long-term and periodic | Continuous
Developed by | Peter Drucker | F.W. Taylor (principle)
Use | Planning, motivation, appraisal | Control, time saving
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 4.1 Staffing: Meaning and Importance
notes.content:
• Staffing: the managerial function of filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure by identifying workforce requirements, recruiting, selecting, placing, training, developing, appraising and compensating people. (Koontz: "filling the positions in the organisation structure through identifying workforce requirements, inventorying the people available, recruitment, selection, placement, promotion, appraisal, compensation and training of needed people.")
• Nature: an important managerial function; pervasive (all managers at all levels); continuous; people-oriented; a part of human resource management (HRM) — staffing is narrower than HRM, as HRM also covers industrial relations, welfare, grievances and collective bargaining.
• Importance: obtains competent personnel for various jobs; ensures higher performance through proper selection and training; continuous survival and growth (succession planning); optimum utilisation of human resources (avoids over-/ under-staffing); improves job satisfaction and morale; basis for all other functions; reduces labour turnover and absenteeism; helps in human resource development.
• Staffing process: (1) estimating manpower requirements (human resource planning); (2) recruitment; (3) selection; (4) placement and orientation (induction); (5) training and development; (6) performance appraisal; (7) promotion and career planning; (8) compensation.
• Staffing as part of HRM; difference: staffing vs HRM — HRM is broader; staffing covers acquisition and development while HRM includes motivation, relations and welfare.

notes.title: 4.2 Human Resource Planning (HRP)
notes.content:
• HRP: the process of forecasting the organisation's future demand and supply of human resources and developing plans to match them so that the right number of people with the right skills are available at the right time and place.
• Objectives: to avoid shortage and surplus; to ensure optimum use of personnel; to plan for expansion, diversification and technology; to help in recruitment, training and development; to control labour costs; succession planning.
• Process:
– 1. Analyse organisational objectives and plans.
– 2. Forecast demand for human resources — methods: managerial judgement, Delphi technique, work-load analysis, work-study (method) technique, ratio-trend analysis, regression analysis, simulation, productivity ratios.
– 3. Forecast supply: internal (skills inventory, replacement charts, Markov analysis, turnover, absenteeism, promotion) and external (labour market, population, education).
– 4. Compare demand and supply — find surplus or shortage.
– 5. Develop action plans — surplus: hiring freeze, retraining, transfer, voluntary retirement, lay-off, retrenchment; shortage: recruitment, overtime, training, outsourcing.
– 6. Implement, monitor and evaluate.
• Job analysis: the systematic study of a job to find its duties, tasks, responsibilities and the skills needed. Outputs: Job description (what the job involves — title, duties, responsibilities, working conditions, reporting) and Job specification (the qualifications, skills, experience, personality and physical traits required of the jobholder). Job design, job evaluation (ranking, grading, point, factor comparison) — used for pay.

notes.title: 4.3 Recruitment
notes.content:
• Recruitment: the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs in the organisation. (Edwin Flippo: "the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating and encouraging them to apply for jobs in an organisation.") It is a positive process; selection is a negative (rejecting) process.
• Sources:
– Internal sources: promotions, transfers, job rotation, retired employees/ re-employment, employee referrals, internal job posting, former employees, dependents of deceased/ disabled employees. Merits: motivation, economical, reliable, quick, no induction needed. Demerits: limited choice, no new blood, internal politics, discourages competition.
– External sources: direct recruitment (notice board), advertisement (newspapers, online), employment exchanges, campus recruitment, placement agencies/ headhunters/ consultancies, walk-in interviews, e-recruitment/ job portals (Naukri, LinkedIn), social media, labour contractors, trade unions, recommendations, casual callers, outsourcing, gig platforms. Merits: fresh ideas, wider choice, skills. Demerits: costly, time-consuming, demotivates existing employees, risk of wrong selection.
• Methods: direct, indirect (advertisement), third-party (agencies).
• Recruitment vs selection:
[TABLE]
Basis | Recruitment | Selection
Meaning | Searching and attracting candidates | Choosing the best from applicants
Nature | Positive | Negative (rejection)
Objective | Create a large pool of applicants | Pick suitable persons
Process | Precedes selection | Follows recruitment
Result | Applications | Appointment/ contract
[/TABLE]
• Factors affecting recruitment: image of the company, job requirements, cost, labour market conditions, government policy (reservation, labour laws), trade union, working conditions, pay.

notes.title: 4.4 Selection
notes.content:
• Selection: the process of choosing the most suitable candidates from the pool of applicants.
• Steps in the selection process:
– 1. Preliminary screening (scrutiny of applications/ preliminary interview).
– 2. Application blank (form) and CV.
– 3. Selection tests: aptitude tests (intelligence/ mental ability, numerical, verbal, mechanical), personality tests (projective, inventories), interest tests, proficiency/ achievement (trade) tests, situational/ job-simulation tests, psychometric tests, group discussion, assessment centres.
– 4. Interview: types — structured, unstructured, panel, stress, behavioural (situational), telephonic, video, group, one-to-one, depth.
– 5. Background/ reference check.
– 6. Medical (physical) examination.
– 7. Final selection and job offer; appointment letter.
– 8. Placement and orientation (induction).
• Qualities of a good test: validity, reliability, objectivity, standardisation.
• Differences: selection vs placement — placement is putting the selected person on the right job.

notes.title: 4.5 Employee Orientation (Induction) and Training
notes.content:
• Orientation (induction): the introduction of a new employee to the organisation, job, colleagues, rules, culture and policies, to reduce anxiety and speed adjustment. Contents: company history, vision, policies, benefits, safety, work rules, facilities, tour, job duties, introduction to supervisors; buddy system, mentoring. Advantages: reduces turnover, saves time, builds loyalty, clear expectations.
• Training: a short-term, job-specific process to improve skills and knowledge for the present job. Development: a long-term, career-oriented process aimed at future roles and overall growth (managerial and conceptual skills). Education: theoretical learning.
[TABLE]
Basis | Training | Development
Focus | Present job | Future job/ career
Term | Short | Long
Target | Employees at operational level | Managers
Nature | Skill-based; reactive | Knowledge/ attitude-based; proactive
Initiative | Usually by the organisation | Often self-driven
[/TABLE]
• Need and importance of training: improves performance and productivity; reduces wastage and accidents; reduces supervision; builds morale; helps adapt to technology; reduces turnover; prepares for promotion; enhances quality; bridges the gap between required and actual performance.
• Training process: (1) identify training needs (organisational, task, person analysis); (2) set objectives; (3) design the programme; (4) implement; (5) evaluate (Kirkpatrick's four levels — reaction, learning, behaviour, results); (6) feedback.
• Methods:
– On-the-job: coaching, job rotation, understudy, apprenticeship, internship, job instruction training (JIT), mentoring, committee assignments. Merits: practical, economical, learning by doing; demerits: disrupts work, poor trainer, damage/ errors.
– Off-the-job: lectures/ classroom, case study, role play, simulation, vestibule training, conferences/ seminars, programmed instruction, e-learning/ virtual reality, management games, sensitivity (T-group) training, in-basket exercise, workshops. Merits: focused; demerits: costly, transfer problems.
• Management development programmes: job rotation, understudy, coaching, multiple management, action learning, case studies, role playing, MDPs at institutes.
• Apprenticeship Act, 1961 (India); Skill India Mission.

notes.title: 4.6 Performance Appraisal Methods
notes.content:
• Performance appraisal: the systematic evaluation of an employee's job performance and potential against set standards. Objectives: pay decisions, promotion, transfer, training needs, feedback, motivation, career planning, validating selection.
• Process: (1) set performance standards; (2) communicate; (3) measure performance; (4) compare; (5) discuss and give feedback; (6) take action.
• Traditional methods:
– Ranking method: employees ranked from best to worst.
– Paired comparison: each employee compared with every other employee in pairs; N(N−1)/2 comparisons.
– Grading: classes (A, B, C).
– Forced distribution: fixed percentages in each category (bell-curve).
– Graphic rating scale: traits rated on a scale (1–5).
– Checklist and weighted checklist.
– Essay (free-form) method.
– Critical incident method: records of significant positive/ negative behaviour.
– Field review method; confidential report (used in government); forced choice; group appraisal.
• Modern methods:
– Management by Objectives (MBO).
– Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS): combines graphic scale and critical incidents with behavioural anchors.
– 360-degree appraisal: feedback from supervisors, peers, subordinates, customers and self.
– Assessment centre method: simulations, tests, exercises by assessors.
– Human resource accounting method: cost and contribution of employees.
– Balanced scorecard, KRA/ KPI-based appraisal, 720-degree, 540-degree, psychological appraisal, 9-box grid, OKRs.
• Errors in appraisal: halo effect, horn effect, central tendency, leniency, strictness, recency effect, similar-to-me bias, personal bias/ stereotyping, spillover effect.
• Characteristics of a good appraisal system: relevant, reliable, valid, objective, transparent, regular, participative, and linked to rewards; feedback is vital.
• Promotion and compensation (briefly): promotion — upward movement with more pay and responsibility (based on merit, seniority or both); compensation — wages, salary, incentives, benefits (fringe benefits).

notes.title: 5.1 Directing: Meaning, Elements and Leadership
notes.content:
• Directing: the managerial function of instructing, guiding, supervising, communicating with and motivating people to achieve organisational objectives — "the heart of management". Koontz: "the interpersonal aspect of managing by which subordinates understand and effectively and efficiently contribute to attainment of enterprise objectives."
• Features: initiates action; pervasive; continuous; flows from top to bottom; human-oriented.
• Elements: supervision, motivation, leadership, communication. Principles: harmony of objectives, maximum individual contribution, unity of command, appropriateness of direction, direct supervision, effective communication, use of informal organisation, leadership, follow-through.
• Importance: initiates action; integrates efforts; motivates; provides stability; coping with change; efficient use of resources.
• Leadership: the process of influencing and inspiring people to work willingly and enthusiastically towards group goals. (Koontz: "the art or process of influencing people so that they will strive willingly and enthusiastically toward the achievement of group goals"; Keith Davis: "the ability to persuade others to seek defined objectives enthusiastically.")
– Features: influence; followers; common goals; situational; continuous process; personal qualities; two-way relationship.
– Importance: initiates action, motivates, provides guidance, creates confidence, builds morale, builds work environment, coordinates, manages change.
– Qualities of a good leader: physical features, knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skills, motivation skills, self-confidence, decisiveness, social skills, objectivity.
• Managers vs leaders:
[TABLE]
Basis | Manager | Leader
Focus | Planning, organising, controlling | Influencing, inspiring
Source of power | Formal position | Personal influence/ followers' acceptance
Orientation | Short-term, stability | Long-term, change and vision
Approach | Administers, maintains | Innovates, develops
Question | How and when? | What and why?
Followers | Subordinates | Followers by choice
Risk | Avoids | Takes risks
[/TABLE]
• Leadership vs management: every manager need not be a leader; every leader need not be a manager; ideal manager is both.

notes.title: 5.2 Leadership Styles
notes.content:
• Four common styles:
– 1. Autocratic (authoritarian): the leader takes all decisions alone and expects obedience; centralised authority; one-way communication. Merits: quick decisions, discipline, clear direction in crisis; demerits: low morale, no initiative, resentment, absenteeism and turnover. Suited for unskilled, uneducated workers or emergencies.
– 2. Democratic (participative): decisions are taken after consulting and involving the group; two-way communication; delegation. Merits: high morale, creativity, commitment, job satisfaction; demerits: slow, may cause indecision; suitable for skilled, educated, motivated teams.
– 3. Laissez-faire (free-rein): leader gives complete freedom to the group to decide; minimum interference; Merits: high autonomy, creativity in experts; demerits: lack of direction, confusion, lack of coordination.
– 4. Paternalistic: the leader acts like a father figure, caring for the welfare of subordinates but taking decisions himself; expects loyalty. Merits: loyalty, harmony; demerits: dependency, stifles initiative.
• Other styles: transformational (inspires and changes followers — Bass, Burns), transactional (reward-punishment exchange), charismatic, servant, bureaucratic, situational, coaching, visionary, pacesetting.
• Factors for style selection: nature of task; followers' maturity; leader's personality; organisational culture; time; situation.

notes.title: 5.3 Theories of Leadership
notes.content:
• 1. Trait theory (Great Man theory): leaders are born with certain traits (intelligence, height, charisma, confidence, integrity, decisiveness, sociability). Critique: no single set of traits; ignores situation and followers.
• 2. Behavioural theories (leaders are made by behaviour):
– Ohio State studies (1945): two dimensions — initiating structure (task orientation) and consideration (people orientation).
– University of Michigan studies: employee-centred vs production-centred leaders.
– Lewin's studies: autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire.
– Blake and Mouton's Managerial Grid (1964): two axes — concern for people and concern for production (1 to 9 scale):
  1,1 Impoverished (low–low); 9,1 Authority–compliance (task); 1,9 Country club (people); 5,5 Middle-of-the-road; 9,9 Team management (high–high — the ideal).
– Likert's four systems: exploitative-authoritative, benevolent-authoritative, consultative, participative.
• 3. Contingency (situational) theories:
– Fiedler's contingency model (1967): leadership effectiveness depends on match between style and situation. Style measured by LPC (Least Preferred Co-worker) scale — high LPC = relationship-oriented; low LPC = task-oriented. Situational favourableness is determined by leader–member relations, task structure and position power. Task-oriented leaders perform best in very favourable or very unfavourable situations; relationship-oriented ones in moderate.
– Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership: style depends on the maturity (readiness) of followers — telling (S1), selling (S2), participating (S3), delegating (S4).
– House's path–goal theory: the leader's job is to clear the path to goals — directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented styles, depending on subordinates and the task.
– Vroom–Yetton–Jago decision model.
• 4. Modern theories: Transformational leadership (idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration), transactional leadership, charismatic leadership, servant leadership, authentic leadership, leader–member exchange (LMX) theory, emotional intelligence (Goleman).

notes.title: 5.4 Motivation
notes.content:
• Motivation: the process of stimulating people to take action to accomplish goals — the inner force that drives behaviour. (Robert Dubin: "the complex of forces starting and keeping a person at work.") Motive = inner drive; motivation = process; motivator = tool.
• Features: psychological/ internal; goal-directed; complex; a continuous process; positive or negative; unlimited needs.
• Importance: improves performance and productivity; reduces absenteeism and turnover; creates a positive attitude; achieves organisational goals; facilitates change; develops team spirit.
• Motivation process: unsatisfied need → tension/ drive → search behaviour → need satisfied → reduction of tension (and a new need arises).
• Types of motivation: intrinsic (from within — interest, achievement) vs extrinsic (external — pay, reward). Positive vs negative motivation.
• Financial incentives: wages, bonus, profit sharing, commission, stock options, perquisites. Non-financial: status, recognition, job security, job enrichment, participation, delegation, autonomy, praise, career opportunities, working conditions.

notes.title: 5.5 Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs Theory
notes.content:
• Abraham Maslow (1943), "A Theory of Human Motivation": needs arranged in a hierarchy of five levels; a satisfied need is no longer a motivator — people move to the next level.
[TABLE]
Level | Need | Examples in the workplace
1 | Physiological (basic) | Food, water, shelter, salary, rest breaks
2 | Safety (security) | Job security, safe conditions, pension, insurance
3 | Social (belonging) | Friendship, team work, acceptance, group membership
4 | Esteem | Recognition, status, promotion, respect, titles
5 | Self-actualisation | Growth, creativity, achieving one's potential, challenging work
[/TABLE]
• Assumptions: needs are in order of priority; unsatisfied needs motivate; a person moves up when lower needs are satisfied; levels 1–2 are lower-order, 3–5 higher-order.
• Criticism: rigid hierarchy not universal; cultural differences; needs may overlap; lack of empirical support; different individuals have different priorities; self-actualisation is vague.
• Application: managers should identify the dominant need of each employee and offer matching rewards.

notes.title: 5.6 McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
notes.content:
• Douglas McGregor (1960), "The Human Side of Enterprise": two sets of assumptions about human nature.
[TABLE]
Basis | Theory X | Theory Y
View of employees | Dislike work and avoid it | Work is as natural as play or rest
Direction | Need to be coerced, controlled, directed | Self-direction and self-control
Responsibility | Avoid responsibility | Seek and accept responsibility
Motivators | Money, security, threats | Higher-order needs — esteem and self-actualisation
Style | Autocratic | Participative/ democratic
Control | Close supervision | Management by objectives, delegation
Suitable for | Unskilled, routine work | Skilled, creative work
[/TABLE]
• Theory Z (William Ouchi): Japanese-style — long-term employment, consensus decision making, collective responsibility, holistic concern.
• Critique: McGregor's X and Y are extremes; the same person may behave differently in different situations.

notes.title: 5.7 Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory
notes.content:
• Frederick Herzberg (1959), "The Motivation to Work" — based on interviews with 200 engineers and accountants; the factors that cause satisfaction are different from those that cause dissatisfaction.
[TABLE]
Hygiene (maintenance/ extrinsic) factors | Motivators (intrinsic) factors
Company policy and administration | Achievement
Supervision | Recognition
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Hygiene (maintenance/ extrinsic) factors | Motivators (intrinsic) factors
Salary | The work itself
Interpersonal relations | Responsibility
Working conditions | Advancement/ promotion
Job security, status | Growth and personal development
[/TABLE]
• Hygiene factors: their absence causes dissatisfaction, but their presence does not motivate (only prevents dissatisfaction) — they bring employees to a "neutral" state.
• Motivators: their presence causes satisfaction and motivation; absence means no satisfaction (but not dissatisfaction).
• Implication: satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not opposites — the opposite of satisfaction is "no satisfaction" and the opposite of dissatisfaction is "no dissatisfaction". Managers must first ensure hygiene factors and then use job enrichment (vertical loading).
• Criticism: based on a small sample (engineers and accountants); method-bound (people credit themselves for satisfaction and blame others); ignores individual differences; pay can be a motivator.
• Herzberg vs Maslow: hygiene ≈ lower-order needs (levels 1–3); motivators ≈ higher-order (levels 4–5).

notes.title: 5.8 Vroom's Expectancy Theory and Other Theories
notes.content:
• Victor Vroom (1964), "Work and Motivation": a person's motivation depends on the expected outcome of effort.
– Motivation (Force) = Valence × Expectancy × Instrumentality (some write F = V × E).
– Expectancy: belief that effort will lead to performance (effort → performance).
– Instrumentality: belief that performance will lead to a reward (performance → outcome).
– Valence: the value or attractiveness of the reward to the individual.
– If any of the three is zero, motivation is zero. Managers should: ensure employees can perform (training), link rewards to performance, offer rewards that employees value.
– Criticism: complex; difficult to measure; assumes rational calculation.
• Other theories (for completeness):
– Alderfer's ERG theory: Existence, Relatedness, Growth; frustration–regression principle.
– McClelland's achievement theory: need for achievement (nAch), power (nPow), affiliation (nAff).
– Adams' equity theory: people compare their input–outcome ratio with others'; perceived inequity leads to adjustment.
– Skinner's reinforcement theory: behaviour is shaped by consequences — positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment, extinction.
– Locke's goal-setting theory: specific and challenging goals with feedback improve performance.
– Porter–Lawler model, Hackman–Oldham job characteristics model.
• Motivation techniques: job enrichment, job enlargement, job rotation, MBO, participation, quality of work life, recognition programmes, incentive schemes, ESOPs.
• Communication (an element of directing): the exchange of information between a sender and a receiver. Process: sender → encoding → message → channel/ medium → decoding → receiver → feedback; noise. Types: formal/ informal; vertical/ horizontal/ diagonal; verbal (oral, written) and non-verbal; barriers: semantic, psychological, organisational, personal, physical/ technological. Overcoming: clarity, feedback, active listening, simple language.
• Supervision: direct watch over subordinates' work; supervisor's roles — link between management and workers, guide, discipline, motivator.

notes.title: 6.1 Controlling: Meaning, Definition, Features and Importance
notes.content:
• Controlling: the managerial function of measuring and correcting performance to make sure that enterprise objectives and plans are accomplished. Koontz: "the measurement and correction of the performance of activities of subordinates in order to make sure that enterprise objectives and the plans devised to attain them are being accomplished." Fayol: "In an undertaking, control consists in verifying whether everything occurs in conformity with the plan adopted, the instructions issued and principles established. Its object is to point out weaknesses and errors in order to rectify them and prevent recurrence." Robert Anthony: management control is the process by which managers assure that resources are obtained and used effectively and efficiently in accomplishing the organisation's objectives.
• Features: goal-oriented; pervasive (all levels and organisations); continuous process; backward as well as forward looking; a dynamic process; relates to planning (closely linked); involves measurement; a positive function (not just fault-finding); every manager's responsibility; action-oriented.
• Importance: accomplishes organisational goals; judges the accuracy of standards; makes efficient use of resources; improves employee motivation; ensures order and discipline; facilitates coordination; reduces risk; detects errors and frauds.
• Planning–controlling relationship: "inseparable twins"; planning is prescriptive (looks ahead), control is evaluative (looks back); planning sets the standards, controlling checks the achievement; plans without controls are useless; control without plans is meaningless; planning is a precondition; controlling is a post-condition.
• Limitations: difficulty in setting quantitative standards; little control over external factors; resistance from employees; costly (time and money); needs trained staff; may lead to short-termism.

notes.title: 6.2 The Controlling Process
notes.content:
• Step 1: Establishing standards — criteria against which actual performance is measured. Types: quantitative (sales, production, cost, time), qualitative (service quality, brand image). Criteria should be specific, measurable and achievable; critical points (key result areas — KRAs). Standards can be physical, cost, revenue, capital, programme, intangible, and benchmarking against the best.
• Step 2: Measurement of actual performance — personal observation, sample checking, performance reports, statistical analysis, and management information system (MIS); objectivity and timeliness are needed.
• Step 3: Comparing actual performance with standards — find the deviation; range of tolerance and critical points.
• Step 4: Analysing deviations — find the cause; controllable vs uncontrollable; critical points require immediate action; management by exception.
• Step 5: Taking corrective action — remedial actions, or revision of standards if unrealistic; no action if deviation is within tolerance; feedback to planning.
• Control cycle is continuous — the process is a feedback loop.

notes.title: 6.3 Essentials of a Sound Control System
notes.content:
• Suitability (appropriateness) — suited to the nature and needs of the organisation and the activity.
• Simplicity (understandability) — easily understood by all concerned.
• Economy — the cost of control should be less than the benefits.
• Flexibility — adaptable to changes in plans and environment.
• Timeliness — information in time for corrective action (forward-looking, quick feedback).
• Objectivity and accuracy — based on facts and measurable standards.
• Focus on critical points (strategic control points) — where deviations matter most.
• Management by exception.
• Acceptability — acceptance by employees; integration with plans and organisation structure; forward-looking; corrective action (indicates who and how); balance; multiplicity of standards (not one).

notes.title: 6.4 Types of Control
notes.content:
• By timing:
– Feedforward (preliminary/ steering) control: applied before the activity — anticipates problems (inputs — quality of raw material, budgets, training, preventive maintenance). Concurrent (real-time/ yes–no) control: applied during the activity — direct supervision, quality checks on the shop floor, automatic controls. Feedback (post-action) control: applied after the activity — compares results to standards (financial statements, audits, performance appraisal).
• By level: strategic control (top-level; long-term — overall performance), tactical (middle level), operational (day-to-day).
• By nature: Preventive vs corrective; bureaucratic vs organic (clan) control; market control; financial control, quality control, inventory control, production control, cost control, personnel/ HR control, marketing control.

notes.title: 6.5 Tools and Techniques of Control
notes.content:
• Traditional techniques:
– Personal observation (management by walking around).
– Statistical reports (graphs, tables, trend analysis).
– Budgetary control: a budget is a plan expressed in numbers. Types: sales budget, production budget, cash budget, capital expenditure, master budget, fixed vs flexible budget, zero-based budgeting (ZBB), performance budget. Benefits: coordination, standards for control, cost control; limitations: rigidity, difficult to forecast, time-consuming.
– Standard costing and variance analysis: compare standard cost with actual cost; variances: material (price, usage), labour (rate, efficiency), overhead; favourable (F) vs adverse (A). Example: standard material cost Rs 10 per unit × 1,000 units = 10,000; actual 11,500 → adverse variance Rs 1,500.
– Break-even analysis: the point where total revenue = total cost (no profit/ no loss). Break-even point (units) = Fixed cost ÷ (Selling price per unit − Variable cost per unit) (contribution per unit); BEP (value) = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio; Margin of safety = Actual sales − BEP sales. Example: FC = Rs 60,000; SP = Rs 50; VC = Rs 30 → contribution Rs 20 → BEP = 3,000 units; BEP sales = Rs 1,50,000. For target profit Rs 20,000: (60,000 + 20,000) ÷ 20 = 4,000 units.
– Ratio analysis: liquidity (current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio), solvency (debt–equity), profitability (gross profit, net profit, return on investment/ ROI = net profit ÷ capital employed × 100), turnover/ activity (inventory turnover, debtors turnover). ROI control.
– Internal audit: an independent appraisal of the operations by the organisation's own staff. Management audit: a systematic evaluation of the management's performance and efficiency.
• Modern techniques:
– PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique) and CPM (Critical Path Method): network techniques to plan, schedule and control projects — critical path = longest path; slack/ float; PERT uses three time estimates — optimistic (a), most likely (m), pessimistic (b); expected time = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6; used in construction and projects. Gantt charts.
– Management Information System (MIS): provides timely and accurate information for decisions and control. ERP, dashboards, data analytics.
– Total Quality Management (TQM): continuous improvement of quality by all (Deming, Juran, Crosby); Six Sigma (defects below 3.4 per million; DMAIC); Kaizen; ISO 9001; just-in-time (JIT); statistical quality control (control charts).
– Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan and Norton): four perspectives — financial, customer, internal business process, learning and growth.
– Responsibility accounting; cost-volume-profit; social audit; benchmarking; OKRs; KPIs; business process re-engineering.
• Behavioural implications of control: employees may resist (fear of exposure; feeling of being watched); overcoming resistance — participation, setting realistic standards, motivation, clear communication, positive attitude, fair application, emphasis on self-control.

notes.title: 7.1 Agile Management
notes.content:
• Agile management: an iterative and incremental approach to managing projects and teams that values flexibility, collaboration, customer feedback and rapid delivery over rigid plans. Originated in software development; the Agile Manifesto (2001) was written by 17 developers at Snowbird, Utah.
• Four values of the Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software (product) over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. (The items on the right are valued, but the items on the left are valued more.)
• 12 principles (summary): satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery; welcome changing requirements; deliver frequently (weeks rather than months); business and developers work together daily; build projects around motivated individuals; face-to-face conversation; working product is the measure of progress; sustainable pace; technical excellence; simplicity; self-organising teams; regular reflection and adaptation (retrospectives).
• Agile frameworks:
– Scrum: work done in fixed-length sprints (1–4 weeks). Roles: Product Owner (maximises value, owns the backlog), Scrum Master (facilitator, removes obstacles), Development Team (cross-functional, self-organising). Events: Sprint planning, daily scrum (stand-up, 15 minutes), sprint review, sprint retrospective. Artefacts: Product backlog, sprint backlog, increment.
– Kanban: visual board (To Do – Doing – Done); limits work-in-progress (WIP); continuous flow.
– Extreme Programming (XP): pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration.
– Lean, SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework), Crystal, DSDM.
• Agile vs Waterfall (traditional):
[TABLE]
Basis | Agile | Waterfall
Approach | Iterative and incremental | Linear and sequential
Planning | Adaptive; changes welcomed | Detailed upfront; changes costly
Customer involvement | Continuous | At the beginning and end
Delivery | Frequent small releases | One final delivery
Documentation | Minimal/ as needed | Extensive
Risk | Detected early | Detected late
[/TABLE]
• Benefits: faster delivery; higher customer satisfaction; flexibility; improved quality; transparency; motivated teams; early risk detection. Challenges: scope creep; need for a cultural shift; difficult in large or regulated environments; dependency on skilled and committed team; less predictability of cost/ time; documentation gaps.
• Beyond software: agile HR, agile marketing, agile manufacturing, and agile leadership (servant leadership, empowerment, psychological safety).

notes.title: 7.2 Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
notes.content:
• CSR: the continuing commitment by business to behave ethically and contribute to economic development while improving the quality of life of the workforce, their families, the local community and society at large. (World Business Council for Sustainable Development.) Howard Bowen — "Father of CSR" (1953, "Social Responsibilities of the Businessman").
• Arguments for CSR: long-term self-interest and improved reputation; avoids government regulation; social stability; better employee morale and retention; investor and consumer preference; resource for social problems; ethical obligation; sustainable development.
• Arguments against (Milton Friedman): "the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits" — shareholders' money; managers lack social expertise; dilutes the profit motive; cost passed to consumers.
• Carroll's CSR pyramid (1991): economic (be profitable) → legal (obey laws) → ethical (do what is right and fair) → philanthropic (be a good corporate citizen).
• Stakeholders: shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, government, community, environment.
• Areas of CSR: environment, education, healthcare, rural development, employee welfare, women's empowerment, ethical sourcing, disaster relief, skill development.
• India's CSR law — Companies Act, 2013, Section 135 and Schedule VII (effective 1 April 2014):
– Applicability: companies with net worth ≥ Rs 500 crore, or turnover ≥ Rs 1,000 crore, or net profit ≥ Rs 5 crore in any of the immediately preceding financial years.
– CSR Committee of the Board (at least 3 directors with one independent director; for companies not required to appoint independent directors, two directors); formulates the CSR policy, recommends the amount, monitors.
– Spend: at least 2% of the average net profits of the company made during the three immediately preceding financial years. Unspent amount: for ongoing projects it is transferred to an Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of the end of the financial year and must be spent within 3 years (otherwise it goes to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days after the third year); for other unspent amounts it is transferred to a Schedule VII fund (e.g. PM CARES, Clean Ganga Fund) within 6 months of the end of the financial year.
– Schedule VII activities: eradicating hunger, poverty and malnutrition; promoting education; gender equality and women's empowerment; environmental sustainability; protection of national heritage; armed forces veterans; sports training; contribution to PM National Relief Fund/ PM CARES; research in science, technology and engineering; slum area development; disaster management; rural development; etc.
– Reporting: disclosure in the Board's report and on the website; impact assessment of projects costing Rs 1 crore or more for companies with an average CSR obligation of Rs 10 crore or more; CSR-1 registration with MCA for implementing agencies.
• India was the first country to mandate CSR spending by law. Examples: Tata Group (education/ health), Infosys Foundation, Reliance Foundation, Mahindra.
• Criticism/ challenges: treated as compliance; greenwashing; lack of impact measurement; fund concentration in some states.
• Related concepts: corporate sustainability, triple bottom line (people, planet, profit — John Elkington), Shared value (Porter), ESG, social audit, philanthropy.

notes.title: 7.3 Business Ethics
notes.content:
• Ethics: the set of moral principles that guide behaviour about what is right and wrong. Business ethics: the application of ethical principles to business — fair, honest and responsible conduct towards all stakeholders.
• Features: based on moral values; concerned with right and wrong; goes beyond legal requirements; relates to stakeholders; voluntary; evolves with society.
• Importance: builds trust and reputation; attracts and retains employees, customers and investors; reduces legal risks and costs; improves decision making; promotes long-term profit; social order; avoids scandals (Enron, Satyam, Volkswagen).
