• Principles/ elements: honesty and integrity; fairness; transparency; accountability; respect for people; compliance with law; confidentiality; avoidance of conflict of interest; social responsibility; environmental concern; customer safety.
• Ethical issues in business: corruption and bribery; insider trading; misleading advertising; product safety; child labour; exploitation; discrimination and harassment; data privacy; environmental damage; whistle-blowing; conflict of interest; accounting frauds; greenwashing; AI ethics; consumer rights.
• Ethical dilemma: a situation requiring a choice between two conflicting moral options.
• Ethical theories: utilitarianism (the greatest good for the greatest number — Bentham, Mill), deontology/ duty-based (Kant — act by moral duty, rules), virtue ethics (Aristotle — character), justice/ rights theory (Rawls — fairness), stakeholder theory (Freeman), shareholder theory (Friedman), egoism; Indian ethics (Gita — Nishkama karma; Kautilya).
• Managing ethics: code of ethics/ conduct; ethics committees; training; ethical leadership (tone at the top); ethical audits; whistle-blower policy (Vigil mechanism in Section 177, Companies Act 2013); ethical decision-making model (identify issue, gather facts, stakeholders, options, test—legal? fair? publicity test, decide, review); corporate governance (board, audit committee, independent directors — SEBI LODR; Sarbanes-Oxley (USA); Clause 49).
• Ethics vs law vs CSR: law — mandatory rules; ethics — moral standards; CSR — voluntary/ mandated contribution to society.
• Indian context: Companies Act 2013, SEBI LODR, Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Consumer Protection Act 2019, Competition Act 2002.

notes.title: 7.4 Green Management
notes.content:
• Green management (environmental management/ sustainable management): integrating environmental concerns into all managerial functions so as to minimise the ecological impact of business activities and ensure sustainable use of resources.
• Drivers: climate change, resource scarcity, regulation (Environment Protection Act 1986; Air and Water Acts), customer awareness, competitive advantage, investor interest (ESG), cost savings, brand image, global agreements (Paris Agreement 2015, net-zero commitments), SDGs (UN 2030).
• Components:
– Green planning: environmental objectives, sustainability strategy, life-cycle assessment.
– Green production/ operations: cleaner production, energy efficiency, renewable energy, waste minimisation, 3Rs — reduce, reuse, recycle, circular economy, eco-design, zero-waste.
– Green marketing: eco-friendly products, eco-labelling, honest environmental claims (avoid greenwashing).
– Green HRM: environmental training, green jobs, paperless work, work from home, green incentives.
– Green finance: green bonds, ESG investment, carbon credits.
– Green supply chain: sustainable sourcing, green logistics, reverse logistics.
– Green accounting and reporting: environmental audit, carbon footprint, Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) by SEBI for top listed companies; Global Reporting Initiative (GRI).
• Standards and tools: ISO 14001 (Environmental Management System), EMAS, LEED (green buildings), Energy Star, BEE star ratings, Eco-mark (India), Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), Carbon trading and Indian Carbon Market.
• Benefits: lower costs (energy/ waste), regulatory compliance, brand reputation, innovation, employee morale, access to green finance. Challenges: high initial investment; lack of awareness; greenwashing; technology; consumers' price sensitivity; measurement difficulties.
• Examples: solar-powered factories, ITC's "carbon positive," Tata Steel's emission reduction, Patagonia, IKEA's sustainability, electric vehicles (Tata Motors), India's "LiFE – Lifestyle for Environment" mission.
• ESG: Environmental, Social, Governance criteria used by investors.

notes.title: 7.5 Organisation Culture
notes.content:
• Organisational culture: the shared values, beliefs, assumptions, norms and practices that shape how people behave in an organisation — "the way we do things around here". (Edgar Schein: "a pattern of shared basic assumptions that the group learned as it solved problems of external adaptation and internal integration.")
• Characteristics (Robbins' seven): innovation and risk taking; attention to detail; outcome orientation; people orientation; team orientation; aggressiveness; stability.
• Levels of culture (Schein): (1) Artefacts — visible (dress, office layout, logos, rituals); (2) Espoused values — stated values, strategies, goals; (3) Basic underlying assumptions — unconscious beliefs.
• Functions: gives identity; creates commitment; stabilises the social system; guides behaviour (control mechanism); facilitates coordination; improves performance; attracts and retains talent.
• Types:
– Charles Handy: power culture (centralised — small firms), role culture (rules and structure — bureaucracies), task culture (team/ project — matrix), person culture (individuals — consultants).
– Cameron and Quinn (Competing Values Framework): clan (family-like, collaborative), adhocracy (innovative, dynamic), market (results-oriented, competitive), hierarchy (controlled, structured).
– Others: strong vs weak culture; dominant culture vs subcultures; Deal and Kennedy: tough-guy macho, work-hard play-hard, bet-your-company, process culture; Hofstede's national culture dimensions — power distance, individualism vs collectivism, masculinity vs femininity, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation, indulgence.
• Creating and sustaining culture: founders' vision and values; selection of employees who fit; top management actions (role models); socialisation (induction, mentoring); stories, rituals, symbols, language; reward systems; policies.
• Changing culture: needs diagnosis, leadership commitment, communication, restructuring, new rewards, training, symbolic changes, patience; challenges — resistance, long time.
• Strong culture vs weak: strong culture — shared deeply, high behavioural control, higher commitment; but may cause resistance to change, groupthink and barriers to diversity.
• Organisation culture vs organisation climate: culture — deep and lasting (values and assumptions); climate — perceptions of the current environment, short-term, changeable.
• Culture and performance: high-performance cultures align values with strategy (Google, Tata — "ethics and trust", Infosys — "C-LIFE", Toyota — kaizen culture); toxic culture leads to scandals (Enron, Wells Fargo, Volkswagen emissions).
